_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a short illustration. 'nonstandard': forms hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.label: Present
entries.usage: Now or regularly.
entries.example: Ich spiele Fußball.

entries.label: sein (present)
entries.usage: 'to be'.
entries.example: Ich bin müde.

entries.label: haben (present)
entries.usage: 'to have'.
entries.example: Ich habe Zeit.

entries.label: Modal verbs
entries.usage: can / must / want + infinitive.
entries.example: Ich kann schwimmen.

entries.label: Perfect (haben)
entries.usage: Finished past with haben.
entries.example: Ich habe gegessen.

entries.label: Perfect (sein)
entries.usage: Past with sein — motion/change.
entries.example: Sie ist gegangen.

entries.label: Präteritum
entries.usage: The written past tense.
entries.example: Er ging nach Hause.

entries.label: Konjunktiv II
entries.usage: Would / were / had — hypotheticals.
entries.example: Ich hätte gern Kaffee.

entries.label: Passive
entries.usage: The action done to the subject.
entries.example: Das Haus wird gebaut.

entries.label: Stem changes
entries.usage: Some common verbs swap their vowel, but only when you talk about 'you' or 'he/she/it'.
entries.example: Du sprichst sehr gut Deutsch. — You speak German very well.

entries.point: Simple past of sein & haben (war, hatte)
entries.label: war / hatte
entries.usage: Saying somebody was somewhere or had something — the everyday past of these two verbs.
entries.example: Gestern war ich sehr müde. — Yesterday I was very tired.

entries.label: Separable verbs
entries.usage: Some verbs split in two, and the front piece jumps to the end of the sentence.
entries.example: Ich stehe jeden Tag um sieben Uhr auf. — I get up at seven every day.

entries.label: Reflexive verbs
entries.usage: Verbs that need an extra little word pointing back at whoever is doing it.
entries.example: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende. — I'm looking forward to the weekend.

entries.label: Imperative
entries.usage: Telling somebody to do something — with a different form for each way of saying 'you'.
entries.example: Sprich bitte langsamer! — Speak more slowly, please!

entries.label: Plusquamperfekt
entries.usage: Something that had already happened before another moment in the past.
entries.example: Als du ankamst, hatte ich schon gegessen. — When you arrived, I had already eaten.

entries.label: hätte … gemacht
entries.usage: What would have happened, but didn't.
entries.example: Wenn ich Zeit gehabt hätte, wäre ich gekommen. — If I had had time, I would have come.

entries.label: Reported speech (er sei)
entries.usage: Repeating what someone else said the way news reports do, without vouching for it.
entries.example: Er sagt, er sei krank. — He says he is ill.

entries.point: Passive alternatives (man, sich lassen, sein + zu)
entries.label: Passive alternatives
entries.usage: Saying what gets done without naming who does it, in the ways Germans prefer to the passive.
entries.example: Man spricht hier Deutsch. — German is spoken here. (one speaks…)

entries.label: V2 word order
entries.usage: The verb sits in slot two of a statement, whatever you choose to start with.
entries.example: Heute lerne ich Deutsch. — Today I am learning German.

entries.point: Es gibt — there is / there are
entries.label: es gibt
entries.usage: Saying that something exists or is around, one thing or many.
entries.example: Es gibt einen Park in der Nähe. — There is a park nearby.

entries.label: Question words
entries.usage: Asking where, how, what, when or why, with the verb right behind.
entries.example: Wo wohnst du? — Where do you live?

entries.label: weil / dass
entries.usage: Adding a because- or that-half, which throws its verb right to the end.
entries.example: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin. — I'm staying home because I'm ill.

entries.label: zu + infinitive
entries.usage: Hanging a second verb on the first — trying to sleep, or doing something in order to.
entries.example: Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Wien zu arbeiten. — I'm learning German in order to work in Vienna.

entries.label: Connectors
entries.usage: Joining two thoughts with so, nevertheless or in order that — each shuffles the words differently.
entries.example: Es regnet, deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause. — It's raining, so we're staying home.

entries.label: Verb + preposition
entries.usage: Verbs welded to a little word — waiting for, thinking of — and the darauf and worauf forms that stand in for what follows.
entries.example: Ich warte auf den Bus. — I'm waiting for the bus.

entries.label: Advanced connectors
entries.usage: Joining thoughts the way careful writing does: by doing something, the more the better, provided that.
entries.example: Man lernt eine Sprache, indem man sie spricht. — You learn a language by speaking it.

entries.label: Modal particles
entries.usage: The tiny words that add a shrug, a nudge or a bit of impatience without changing what is said.
entries.example: Komm doch mit, es wird lustig! — Do come along, it'll be fun!

entries.label: Accusative
entries.usage: The direct object.
entries.example: Ich sehe den Mann.

entries.label: Dative
entries.usage: The indirect object; after certain prepositions.
entries.example: Ich gebe dem Kind das Buch.

entries.label: Genitive
entries.usage: Possession: of.
entries.example: das Auto des Mannes

entries.label: Adjective endings
entries.usage: Adjective endings by case, gender, article.
entries.example: ein roter Wagen, den roten Wagen

entries.label: Two-way prepositions
entries.usage: Accusative for motion, dative for place.
entries.example: in die Stadt / in der Stadt

entries.label: Possessive articles
entries.usage: mein/dein/sein decline like ein.
entries.example: mein Bruder, meinem Bruder

entries.label: Subject pronouns
entries.usage: The words for I, you, he, she, we and they when they are the one doing something.
entries.example: Ich wohne in Berlin. — I live in Berlin.

entries.label: Object pronouns
entries.usage: The words for me, you, him and them when they are on the receiving end instead.
entries.example: Ich liebe dich. — I love you.

entries.label: Gender & plural
entries.usage: Whether a thing counts as a der, die or das word, and how it turns plural.
entries.example: Ich habe zwei Bücher. — I have two books.

entries.label: der / die / das
entries.usage: The German words for 'the' — learn each one glued to its noun.
entries.example: Das Haus ist groß. — The house is big.

entries.label: ein / eine
entries.usage: The German words for 'a' or 'an', and the plural that simply drops them.
entries.example: Das ist ein Haus. — That is a house.

entries.label: das Gute / ein Reisender
entries.usage: Describing words used as things in their own right: the good, a traveller.
entries.example: Das Gute an der Sache ist der Preis. — The good thing about it is the price.

entries.label: Comparative
entries.usage: Saying one thing is bigger than another, or the biggest of the lot.
entries.example: Berlin ist größer als München. — Berlin is bigger than Munich.

entries.label: nicht / kein
entries.usage: Saying no or not — which of the two you need depends on what you are cancelling.
entries.example: Ich habe kein Auto. — I don't have a car.

entries.label: Relative clauses
entries.usage: Adding a who- or which-part to say more about a person or thing you just named.
entries.example: Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Lehrer. — The man who is standing there is my teacher.

entries.label: Extended attributes
entries.usage: The packed written style that squeezes a whole description in between 'the' and its noun.
entries.example: Die gestern getroffene Entscheidung war richtig. — The decision made yesterday was right.
